sections.title: Before reading: study Chapter 1 in How to read. Then begin the first scene: the wrong book.

segments.text: 安持大書，寧持小書。安持一書，寧持一書。安坐，寧立。安開大書，寧開小書。
人開門，入門。安閉大書，寧閉小書。人視大書，安視人。
寧還小書，安取小書。安得小書，持二書。寧坐，人立。
寧：「小書。」

grammar.title: 安持書

tables.caption: Subject | action | object; read across, not as a memorisation drill
Quantity before the noun; the written noun stays the same

grammar.note_en:
Begin with the Chapter 1 preparation in How to read. Its English meaning cards, shape contrasts and attempts come before this story; these notes consolidate what you have now read. Tap a story character for the contextual English popup. You do not need a picture to follow who carries each book.

A subject is the person or thing a sentence says something about. A verb describes an action or state. An object names a person or thing the verb relates to directly, such as a book being held or a person being seen; it need not be physically changed by the action. In 安持大書, “An holds a large book,” 安 is the subject, 持 the action and 大書 the object. In 寧持小書, “Ning holds a small book,” the subject changes but 持 keeps exactly the same written form. In 人取大書, “the person takes the large book,” the same subject–verb–object order is used. The first table lays those three real story clauses out as a reference. Read complete rows: they are not independent word lists to recite.

安坐 means “An sits”; 寧立 means “Ning stands.” These actions do not require an object. A following noun is therefore not compulsory after every verb. In 入門 and 出門, 門 names the place of movement: into or out through the doorway. It is not an object physically changed by entering or leaving. A bare noun does not contain the English distinction between “a” and “the,” and its written shape does not acquire an English plural ending. In this particular story there are two physical books, one large and one small. No claim about who legally owns them is made.

Size precedes the noun: 大書 means “a large book” and 小書 “a small book.” Number also precedes the noun in the bounded pattern taught here: 一書 means “one book,” 二書 “two books.” In 安持二書, “An holds two books,” 二 gives information that the bare noun alone would not supply. In 安持一書, “An holds one book,” the noun 書 remains unchanged. The second table contrasts those two expressions. This is the chapter’s limited book-counting pattern, not a rule that every later quantity construction will have exactly this form.

Two successive actions can share a clearly named actor. 人取大書出門 means “the person takes the large book and goes out through the doorway”: 取大書 is followed by 出門. 安持小書出門 means “An carries the small book out through the doorway.” The margin separators show those action units; they do not add spoken words. When the next short clause plainly continues the same person, its name can be omitted: 安立，閉小書 means “An stands and closes the small book.” Whenever the actor changes in this chapter, the prose supplies the next name or 人. Do not extend this into permission to guess a subject across an unrelated paragraph.

還 is huán here: return a book to someone’s custody. It is not the later hái “again/still.” 得 dé tells us that someone gains possession; 取 qǔ describes taking. 持 chí tells us who is holding or carrying something. 視 shì is deliberate looking; 見 jiàn is seeing. Those words keep different jobs in following the books. A return or temporary holding does not prove legal ownership. The visitor’s purpose remains unexplained; the reader can nevertheless follow the visible transfers.

The brief quoted fragments are attributed speech. 寧：「小書。」 is Ning’s “The small book.” 人：「小書。」 repeats “The small book,” but the visitor’s next action is 人取大書出門, “the person takes the large book and goes out.” The mismatch between the size word spoken and the book taken is visible in the Chinese; no motive or ownership is inferred. 安：「失大書。」 reports “Lost the large book”; An’s clearly identified voice supplies the understood person who lost custody. Full question constructions come later.

Workbook and Pensa A/B describe additional small incidents, so their sentences need not repeat what happened in the story. Their English cues and taught readings identify the intended form; type Chinese characters, not pinyin. Pensa C instead asks about this story: continue the shown event with a sentence about the person or book after the colon. More than one wording can be valid; compare the event and reference with the self-check model and rubric, rather than copying its precise string.

The final 安得大書，失小書 contrasts the episode’s outcomes: “An got back the large book but lost custody of the small one.” It can summarize what happened; it does not tell us exactly when An noticed or understood the last transfer. The visitor’s permission and purpose remain unstated.

A.title: Pensa A — Keep the pattern while people, sizes and numbers change

obrazec.rule: New incidents. Put size directly before the noun. Cues: 1: small; 2: large; 3: small; 4: large
New incidents. Put the numeral directly before the noun; the noun does not change. Cues: 1: two; 2: one; 3: two; 4: two

B.title: Pensa B — Retrieve the verb named by each cue; the bank has five extras

obrazec.rule: New incidents. The cue identifies the intended studied verb; readings distinguish overlapping meanings. 1: take (qǔ); 2: obtain (dé); 3: lose (shī); 4: enter (rù); 5: go out (chū); 6: return (huán); 7: open (kāi); 8: close (bì)

C.title: Pensa C — Continue each cue with a Chinese sentence about the named person or book. Item 6 concerns the final scene.

items.rubric: Accepts a true complete sentence about Ning in the opening: holding the small book, standing, or opening it. A bare noun or yes/no is insufficient.

Accepts a true next response by An: standing/closing the small book, losing custody of the large one, stopping at the shut door, reporting the loss, or leaving with the small book after the door opens. Do not require this model’s exact wording.
In this first blocked departure, accepts stopping or reporting the lost large book; a fuller answer may continue with the exit after Ning reopens the door.
Accepts taking back or gaining the large book, holding both books, or inspecting the returned large book. Do not claim ownership or guess the visitor’s purpose.
Accepts a complete sentence about Ning taking both books or opening/inspecting the small one after that transfer; both facts are not mandatory in one answer.

Requires a complete, text-supported sentence identifying the visitor taking or carrying the small book away in the final scene. Accept equivalent licensed wording, including separate clauses such as 人取小書。人持小書出門。 Do not accept 安失小書 alone: it does not retrieve who takes the book away. Do not infer ownership, permission or motive.

notes: Original constructed graded narration; no authentic quotation in chapter1. No audio or generated imagery.
Han character counts are shared-kernel atoms, distinct from editorial lexical senses. All introductory preparation and English are excluded from narrative length.

English instructional cues are permitted by RULES.md 2026-11-04. Short closed items use visible English group/reference cues and target Chinese answers. Early open C uses scene-continuation questions, with no unlicensed interrogatives.
The English grammar explanation intentionally exceeds the default note warning: it defines terms from zero Chinese and translates every cited example.
The story is below its unchanged advisory window. No plan, practice, recurrence or destination requirement has been relaxed; independent review must judge actual substance.
